headline: Former White House health aide accuses Trump advisers of catering to special interests
author: Rachel Roubein

paragraphs.text: Calley Means, a former Trump White House adviser who quit last month, accused top administration aides and strategists of catering to special interests, and recommended that the president “clears house” in an extensive interview with podcast host Joe Rogan released Friday.

Means, who also served as a top aide of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., recounted for more than two hours his time inside the administration, frequently naming aides that he alleged blocked or hindered progress on policies popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Means quit his job roughly two weeks ago amid White House delays in enacting some of the food policies he and other top health officials had been seeking.

The interview comes as Democrats had a sweeping electoral victory this week, prompting Republican finger-pointing over the causes of the wipeout. Means claims the architects of Trump’s midterm strategy were “obsessed with redistricting” ahead of the November elections.

Several of Means’s allegations centered on some top Trump aides and allies, including Susie Wiles, his chief of staff, and Tony Fabrizio, Trump’s chief pollster. At one point, he claimed that Wiles blocked one of the health department’s food initiatives out of fear it would hurt political donations from the sugar industry. On Friday, after the podcast was released, Trump announced that Wiles would be replaced as chief of staff by his longtime aide Stephen Miller. Fabrizio did not provide comment.
“It is absolutely true that his administration has been infiltrated by the very people that he energized voters to say he would get out of D.C.,” Means said.

Later in the podcast, he said, “I think President Trump can save this presidency, can change staff, and get back on more of an America First fighting position against the swamp and get a lot done, and maybe even get some things done with Democrats.”
In a statement, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said “the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again.”

“The Administration has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming,” she said. “President Trump and Secretary Kennedy continue to work around the clock to deliver more wins for the American people.”
Some White House officials have countered that Wiles is a MAHA champion, and some of Means’s claims could not immediately be independently verified.

Means claimed that Trump is not fully aware of some of the decisions made by his top staff because he “can’t be everywhere at once,” saying that Trump asked “how the hell did this happen” after the Supreme Court restricted a massive wave of lawsuits against a major pesticide manufacturer. The administration supported the pesticide maker in the case, a switch from the Biden administration.
Means’s criticism of the administration comes as several policy priorities of the MAHA movement — which was born out of the political alignment between Trump and Kennedy — have stalled.

The MAHA movement is composed of multiple and, at times, competing factions, including ones pushing for healthier food, major changes to vaccines and less pesticide use. While at the White House and health department, Means pushed aggressively for MAHA policies, particularly related to food. This includes efforts to get food companies to drop synthetic dyes, changes to the dietary guidelines and advocating for states to adopt rules barring soda and candy from the nation’s food stamps program.

In the podcast interview, Means lamented a lack of midterm messaging around issues central to the MAHA movement, as polling has shown the majority of Americans agree there is insufficient regulation of chemical additives in food and pesticides used to grow crops.
Health and Human Services spokeswoman Emily Hilliard previously pushed back on the notion that Kennedy’s MAHA food agenda has been “stalled or slow walked.”

In his talk with Rogan, Means paints a portrait of White House staff who, at times, sidelined Kennedy and the policies his supporters are pushing. He claimed there was “tremendous energy to diminish [Kennedy’s] impact on the election.”

Democrats and medical experts have hammered some of the policies Kennedy, the founder of a prominent anti-vaccine group, have pursued, such as a sweeping reduction of the childhood vaccine schedule. Shortly after the election, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland) wrote on social media that “RFK Jr. must resign or be fired,” while prominent MAHA leaders argue the party should not seek to oust the nation’s top health official.
Throughout Rogan’s podcast, Means described his account of how key policies were crafted. He contended that Wiles has a “stranglehold” on such decisions.

MAHA activists have particularly been frustrated over the Trump administration’s handling of glyphosate, a widely used weed killer they say contributes to childhood health problems. Kennedy has previously called the herbicide “one of the likely culprits in America’s chronic disease epidemic” and was part of a team that won a $289 million judgment against chemical manufacturer Monsanto, which Bayer acquired in 2018, over claims the weed killer caused cancer.

Means alleges that Kennedy was not consulted on several major administration policies on glyphosate. In one such instance, Means recalled being told to review an executive order to boost production of glyphosate, and says he called the directive a “political disaster.” White House staff, including Wiles, made clear the issue was “not up for discussion,” Means said.
Means says he decided to leave the administration due to a White House delay in releasing the definition of ultra-processed foods and a new school lunch meal.

He also accused Wiles of blocking an initiative aimed at determining the safety of certain ingredients common in ultra-processed foods. The federal health department had been poised earlier this year to conclude that food companies should produce “any detailed safety studies” related to certain ingredients, The Post previously reported.

On immunizations, Means said that Trump advisers had urged Kennedy to avoid talking about vaccines ahead of the midterms. But, he said, Trump “wanted to go hard on investigating vaccines,” and removed the block.

“When President Trump heard about an issue, his inclination was right,” Means said. “And the people around him, I think, treat him horribly. They talk about him like a baby. They say it’s because ‘we’re the political experts.’”

As the Trump administration grapples with election’s fallout, Means argued that a future president should work to get corporate money out of politics. In the meantime, Trump should “go to war with Congress,” as well as meet with some of the progressive senators.

“I think the best chance the president has to get things done is meeting with Bernie, meeting with El-Sayed,” Means said, referring to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan).
